title: On the Myths and Truths About How Girls Learn
author: Rebecca Birch
summary: Rebecca Birch, drawing on eight years working in girls' education and a conference presentation with colleague Cassandra Pride, tests five popular claims about how girls learn against the research evidence. She debunks the idea that girls learn differently from boys (rooted in the long-discredited VARK learning-styles theory) and argues process-product research instead supports universally strong whole-class instruction as most effective for novice learners of either sex. She questions the assumption that girls learn better collaboratively, pointing out that open-ended group work often just redistributes teacher preparation time rather than producing better learning. She finds Dweck-style growth mindset interventions oversold, citing low predictive validity once ability and socioeconomic status are controlled for, and prefers Andrew Martin's evidence-backed 'Growth Goals' alternative. She grants partial truth to concerns about girls' fragility but argues the fragility frame risks becoming self-fulfilling, per Jonathan Haidt's coddling critique, and that practices like cold calling and practice testing build resilience rather than undermine it. Finally, she challenges the claim that girls are better off in co-ed schools, citing evidence that boys receive more teacher attention in mixed classrooms and that behavioral disruptions disproportionately affect girls' learning environment.
points: Birch's rebuttal to the learning-styles myth cites process-product research favoring universally strong whole-class instruction for all novice learners regardless of sex, rather than individualized sensory-preference catering.

Her critique of growth mindset in girls' schools specifically flags its low predictive validity once researchers control for ability and socioeconomic status, and she offers Andrew Martin's 'Growth Goals' as a better-evidenced alternative.

Her fragility-myth analysis draws directly on Jonathan Haidt's 'Coddling of the American Mind' framework, arguing that shielding girls from anxiety-inducing challenges (like cold calling or practice testing for math anxiety) worsens the very fragility schools are trying to prevent.

The co-ed myth rebuttal cites specific mechanisms (boys receive more teacher attention in mixed classrooms; behavioral disruption is more common among boys and affects girls' learning environment) rather than a general assertion that single-sex schooling is superior.
quotes: These ideas stem from the long-debunked learning styles theory, which you may know as VARK (visual, auditory, reading/writing, kinaesthetic).
